cases.title: The flower puzzle
cases.intro: Investigate the base flow, meaning move steadily, like water. A family member keeps a connection to this base and its meaning.

groups.label: flow family
groups.detail: The base and its meaning connect

groups.label: Another base
groups.detail: Similar letters or sounds are not enough

cards.evidence: flow + ed → flowed: moved steadily in the past.
flow + ing → flowing: moving steadily.
over + flow → overflow: flow beyond a limit.
over + flow + ing → overflowing: flowing beyond a limit.
Flower means a bloom. It is not flow + er; the letters do not make that meaning.
flower + s → flowers. The base is flower, not flow.

evidence.prompt: Why is flower outside this flow family?
answers: Its base and meaning are different, even though some letters match.
Every word ending in -er is a person who does something.
A family member must sound exactly like its base.
evidence.explanation: A spelling resemblance is a clue to investigate, not proof. Flower has its own base and word history.

apply.prompt: “Rain made the pond overflow.” What happened?
answers: Water flowed beyond the pond’s limit.
Flowers grew in the pond.
The water stopped moving.
apply.explanation: Over- adds the idea of going beyond a limit to flow.

cases.tip: Use both structure and meaning. Do not cut a word just because a familiar letter string appears.

cases.title: Play or display?
cases.intro: Investigate the base play, meaning take part in a game or activity. A family member keeps a connection to this base and its meaning.

groups.label: play family
groups.detail: The base and its meaning connect

groups.label: Another base
groups.detail: Similar letters or sounds are not enough

cards.evidence: play + er → player: a person who plays.
play + ing → playing: taking part in the activity.
re + play → replay: play again.
play + ful → playful: enjoying play; full of fun.
Display means show. It is not dis + play meaning “not play”.
display + ed → displayed. Its base here is display, not play.

evidence.prompt: What is the strongest evidence that replay belongs?
answers: Re- means again, and the word still means play.
It has the same number of letters as player.
Every word ending in play belongs automatically.
evidence.explanation: Replay has a meaningful prefix plus the base play. Display has a different base and history.

apply.prompt: “Let’s replay the final scene.” What should we do?
answers: Play the scene again.
Stop playing the scene.
Show a poster of the scene.

cases.tip: A word family is based on a meaningful base, not just a matching ending.

cases.title: The missing e
cases.intro: Investigate the base care, meaning look after; give attention. A family member keeps a connection to this base and its meaning.

groups.label: care family
groups.detail: The base and its meaning connect

groups.label: Another base
groups.detail: Similar letters or sounds are not enough

cards.evidence: care + ful → careful: taking care. Keep the final e before -ful.
care + less → careless: not taking enough care.
care + ing → caring: looking after someone. Remove final e before -ing.
care + ed → cared: gave care in the past. Remove final e before -ed.
Scare means frighten. There is no prefix s- meaning “frighten” attached to care.
scare + ed → scared: frightened. Its base is scare, not care.

evidence.prompt: Why does caring still belong to care?
answers: The full base is care; its final e is removed before -ing.
Its base is always car because those letters stay.
Any word starting with car belongs to care.
evidence.explanation: Word sums show the underlying base even when a suffix changes its written ending.

apply.prompt: “A careless spill soaked the notebook.” What does careless tell us?
answers: Someone did not take enough care.
Someone took extra care.
Someone frightened the notebook.
apply.explanation: -less adds the idea of lacking care in this context.

cases.tip: Compare care + ful → careful with care + ing → caring. The base is the same; the suffix boundary behaves differently.

cases.title: Hoping or hopping?
cases.intro: Investigate the base hope, meaning want something good to happen. A family member keeps a connection to this base and its meaning.

groups.label: hope family
groups.detail: The base and its meaning connect

groups.label: Another base
groups.detail: Similar letters or sounds are not enough

cards.evidence: hope + ful → hopeful: feeling hope. Keep final e before -ful.
hope + less → hopeless: without hope.
hope + ing → hoping: wanting something good to happen. Remove final e.
hope + ed → hoped: felt hope in the past. Remove final e.
Hop means jump on one foot or make a small jump. It is a different base.
hop + ing → hopping. Double p at this boundary. It belongs to hop, not hope.

answers: hope + ing → hoping
hop + ing → hoping
hop + ping → hoping
evidence.explanation: Hoping keeps the meaning of hope. Hopping comes from hop and doubles p.

apply.prompt: “Ari is hoping for snow.” What is Ari doing?
answers: Wishing that snow will fall.
Jumping on one foot.
Playing in snow that already fell.
apply.explanation: The spelling and the sentence point to hope, not hop.

cases.tip: Say and compare hoping and hopping. Read the whole sentence before deciding.

cases.title: Heat hidden in wheat?
cases.intro: Investigate the base heat, meaning make warm or hot. A family member keeps a connection to this base and its meaning.

groups.label: heat family
groups.detail: The base and its meaning connect

groups.label: Another base
groups.detail: Similar letters or sounds are not enough

cards.evidence: heat + ed → heated: made warm in the past.
heat + ing → heating: making warm.
re + heat → reheat: heat again.
heat + er → heater: a thing that provides heat.
Wheat is a grain. It is not w + heat; w- is not a meaningful prefix here.
Cheat means act dishonestly. Its base is cheat, not heat.

evidence.prompt: What makes heater a member of the heat family?
answers: It names something that provides heat.
All words ending in -er are people.
Any word with h-e-a-t letters has the base heat.
evidence.explanation: Here -er makes a noun for a thing that does the action. Meaning matters as well as letters.

apply.prompt: “Reheat the soup before lunch.” What should happen?
answers: The soup should be heated again.
Wheat should be added to the soup.
The soup should be cooled.

cases.tip: An -er noun can name a person or a thing. Check what the word means.

cases.title: Two bases can join
cases.intro: Investigate the base corn, meaning the grain we eat. A family member keeps a connection to this base and its meaning.

groups.label: corn family
groups.detail: The base and its meaning connect

groups.label: Another base
groups.detail: Similar letters or sounds are not enough

cards.evidence: pop + corn → popcorn: corn that has popped. This is a compound.
corn + field → cornfield: a field of corn. Both parts are bases.
corn + bread → cornbread: bread made with cornmeal. Both parts are bases.
sweet + corn → sweetcorn: a kind of corn. This is a compound.
Corner means a place where edges meet. It is not corn (the grain) + er.
Unicorn’s corn comes from a Latin word for horn, not the grain corn.

answers: It joins two bases: corn and field.
Field is a suffix meaning person.
Every long word is a compound.
evidence.explanation: Both corn and field can stand as words and contribute meaning. A compound joins bases.

apply.prompt: “We walked beside the cornfield.” What did we walk beside?
answers: A field where corn grows.
A corner of a room.
An animal with one horn.
apply.explanation: Corn + field gives a useful clue to the compound’s meaning.

cases.tip: The grain corn and the Latin element for horn have similar spellings but different meanings and histories.

cases.title: The -er mystery
cases.intro: The ending -er can do different jobs. Read each word and its sentence before deciding.

groups.label: Person who does it
groups.detail: Names someone who does the base action

groups.label: More than another
groups.detail: Compares a quality

cards.evidence: teach + er → teacher: a person who teaches.
run + er → runner: a person who runs. Double n.
bake + er → baker: a person who bakes. Remove final e.
fast + er → faster: more fast.
cards.sentence: The rabbit is faster than the turtle.

cards.evidence: small + er → smaller: less large.
cards.sentence: This box is smaller than that one.

cards.evidence: cold + er → colder: more cold.

evidence.prompt: How can we decide what -er does?
answers: Look at the base, the word’s meaning, and its sentence.
-er always means a person.
-er always means more.
evidence.explanation: The same written ending can serve different grammatical jobs. Context and the kind of base help.

apply.prompt: “This coat is warmer than mine.” What does -er do?
answers: It compares warmth: more warm.
It names a person who warms things.
It means warmth happened in the past.
apply.explanation: Warmer is a comparison here, not a name for a person.

cases.tip: Compare teach → teacher with small → smaller. Ask: a person, or a comparison?

cases.title: The two jobs of -s
cases.intro: An -s ending can mark more than one noun, or a present-tense verb with he, she, it, or one named person. Use the sentences.

groups.label: More than one
groups.detail: Plural noun

groups.label: One subject does it
groups.detail: Present-tense verb

cards.evidence: cat + s → cats: more than one cat.
cards.sentence: Three cats sat on the wall.

cards.evidence: book + s → books: more than one book.
paint + s → paints: more than one kind or container of paint here.
jump + s → jumps: what one named person does.
read + s → reads: what one named person does.
paint + s → paints: what one named person does here.

evidence.prompt: Why are the two paints cards in different groups?
answers: One is a plural noun; the other is a verb in its sentence.
Identical spellings must always have the same job.
The longer sentence always contains a plural.
evidence.explanation: The spelling alone does not settle the job. Read “three paints” and “Noah paints” in context.

apply.prompt: “The dog barks at the door.” What does -s mark?
answers: A present-tense action with one subject: the dog.
More than one dog.
An action in the past.
apply.explanation: Barks is a verb here. The noun dog is singular.

cases.tip: Read aloud: “Three paints are on the shelf” and “Noah paints the fence.” Same spelling, different jobs.

cases.title: What does un- undo?
cases.intro: Un- can mean “not” with a quality, or reverse an action. Investigate its job in each word.

groups.label: Not this quality
groups.detail: Describes the opposite state

groups.label: Reverse the action
groups.detail: Undo what the base action does

cards.evidence: un + happy → unhappy: not happy.
un + fair → unfair: not fair.
un + kind → unkind: not kind.
un + wrap → unwrap: remove the wrapping.
un + tie → untie: undo a knot.
un + lock → unlock: undo the locked state.

answers: No. It can also mean reverse an action, as in untie.
Yes. Untie means never tie anything.
No. Un- always means again.
evidence.explanation: Unhappy describes a state. Untie describes undoing an action. Keep the meaning connected to the base.

apply.prompt: “Please unwrap the gift.” What should you do?
answers: Remove the wrapping.
Wrap it a second time.
Decide that it is not a gift.

cases.tip: Act out wrap/unwrap and tie/untie, then contrast happy/unhappy.

cases.title: One ending, three sounds
cases.intro: These words all use -ed for a past action. Sort by the ending you hear when you say the whole word. /t/ sounds like t; /d/ like d; /ɪd/ adds a syllable, like id.

groups.label: /t/ sound
groups.detail: No extra syllable

groups.label: /d/ sound
groups.detail: No extra syllable

groups.label: /ɪd/ sound
groups.detail: An extra syllable

cards.evidence: jump + ed → jumped. The ending sounds like /t/; it still marks the past.
help + ed → helped. The ending sounds like /t/.
play + ed → played. The ending sounds like /d/.
clean + ed → cleaned. The ending sounds like /d/.
want + ed → wanted. The ending sounds like /ɪd/ and adds a syllable.
need + ed → needed. The ending sounds like /ɪd/ and adds a syllable.

evidence.prompt: What stays the same in these six words?
answers: The -ed spelling and its job of marking a past action.
The ending always sounds exactly the same.
Every ending adds an extra syllable.
evidence.explanation: A morpheme can keep its spelling and grammatical job while its pronunciation varies.

apply.prompt: “We walked home yesterday.” What does -ed tell us?
answers: The walking happened in the past, even though the ending sounds like /t/.
There was more than one walk.
The action is happening now.
apply.explanation: Walk + ed → walked. The suffix marks the past; its sound here is /t/.

cases.tip: Read each whole word. Do not pronounce every -ed as a separate “ed” syllable.
